name: Microplastics on sand: when does a beach look dirty?
description:
Faithful replication of the questionnaire in Asakura, Nakagawa, Shimizu, Yagi & Ussawarujikulchai (2026), "Proposed Threshold for Microplastic Presence on Sandy Beaches Perceived as 'Clean': A Psychological Acceptability Approach", Pollutants 6(2):29 (online panel in Japan, 245 attentive respondents analysed). After six background questions and an attention check ("select polystyrene"), participants see three series of eight photographs of real beach sand in a tray with increasing amounts of crushed plastic (white polypropylene, blue polypropylene, white expanded polystyrene; 0 to 22–55 cm³ per m²) and pick the photograph at which the sand starts to look dirty, or "all are acceptable". Half of respondents found the sand dirty at about 1–2 cm³/m², with no difference between the three plastics. Questionnaire and all 24 photographs from the paper's Appendix A (CC BY 4.0), used with credit; the template is removed if the authors object.

Differences from the original study: (1) English instead of the original Japanese wording (the English text follows Appendix A); (2) a consent page is added; (3) photographs can be tapped to see them larger; (4) the published Appendix A prints the same photograph for blue polypropylene options 6 and 7, so in this template option 7 of the blue series repeats option 6 (the true option 7 photo is not published); (5) option-to-concentration codes are given in each question's description, following the paper's Table 1.
author: Asakura, Nakagawa, Shimizu, Yagi & Ussawarujikulchai

pages.name: intro
pages.intro: Questionnaire on the visually acceptable amount of microplastics on sandy beaches. It has ten short questions and takes about 5 minutes. Answers are anonymous and used for research only.
pages.title: Microplastics on sandy beaches

elements.name: consent
elements.label: I agree to take part in this survey.
elements.title: Consent

elements.name: travel_time
elements.title: How long does it take you to reach the beach from your residence when you go there for leisure or work?

elements.name: visit_frequency
elements.title: How frequently do you visit the beach or the sea?

elements.name: plastic_concern
elements.title: Are you interested in the issue of marine plastic pollution?

elements.name: cleanup_experience
elements.title: Have you ever participated in volunteer activities, events, or self-initiated efforts to pick up litter or clean public spaces?

elements.name: trap_question
elements.title: Which type of plastic do you think has the greatest potential to cause marine pollution? For this question, regardless of your actual opinion, please select polystyrene.
elements.description: Attention check: 4 (polystyrene) = optimizing respondent; the paper analyses optimizing respondents only.

elements.name: white_pp_threshold
elements.title: The following photographs show sand mixed with fine plastic particles (microplastics). The amount of microplastics increases from 1 to 8. Please indicate the number at which you begin to feel that the sand looks dirty (psychologically unacceptable).
elements.description: Eight photographs (Appendix A) of beach sand in a 34 × 24 cm tray with increasing amounts of crushed white polypropylene: options 1–8 = 0, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10,000, 20,000 mg-MPs/m² (volume 0, 0.2, 0.6, 1.1, 2.2, 5.5, 11.0, 22.1 cm³/m²). Value: option number 1–8 at which the sand first looks dirty, 9 = all acceptable. Analysis in the paper: share judging each concentration unacceptable (option ≤ k), 50% point by interpolation; optimizing respondents only (trap_question = 4).

elements.name: blue_pp_threshold
elements.title: The following photographs show sand mixed with a different type of microplastic. The amount of microplastics increases from 1 to 8. Please indicate the number at which you begin to feel that the sand looks dirty (psychologically unacceptable).
elements.description: Eight photographs (Appendix A) of beach sand in a 34 × 24 cm tray with increasing amounts of crushed blue polypropylene: options 1–8 = 0, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10,000, 20,000 mg-MPs/m² (volume 0, 0.2, 0.6, 1.1, 2.2, 5.5, 11.0, 22.1 cm³/m²). Value: option number 1–8 at which the sand first looks dirty, 9 = all acceptable. Analysis in the paper: share judging each concentration unacceptable (option ≤ k), 50% point by interpolation; optimizing respondents only (trap_question = 4). Note: the published Appendix A prints the same photograph for options 6 and 7, so blue_pp_7.jpg repeats blue_pp_6.jpg.

elements.name: white_ps_threshold
elements.title: The following photographs show sand mixed with yet another type of microplastic. The amount of microplastics increases from 1 to 8. Please indicate the number at which you begin to feel that the sand looks dirty (psychologically unacceptable).
elements.description: Eight photographs (Appendix A) of beach sand in a 34 × 24 cm tray with increasing amounts of crushed white expanded polystyrene: options 1–8 = 0, 10, 20, 40, 100, 200, 400, 1000 mg-MPs/m² (volume 0, 0.6, 1.1, 2.2, 5.5, 11.0, 22.1, 55.2 cm³/m²). Value: option number 1–8 at which the sand first looks dirty, 9 = all acceptable. Analysis in the paper: share judging each concentration unacceptable (option ≤ k), 50% point by interpolation; optimizing respondents only (trap_question = 4).
